what: The active address route asks the Planning Portal for one fuzzy-search result and unconditionally treats result 0 as the requested property.
why: Several report and satellite routes call this endpoint. A fuzzy Portal result can therefore attach a neighbour's lot, zoning, height, FSR, and downstream rules to the entered address. The newer lookup deliberately prevents this with exact address-number/street matching.
fix: Request multiple candidates and apply the existing filterToAskedProperty helper before selecting a result; return not-found when none matches. Add a route test with a nearest-but-different street number.

what: Site-specific LEP clauses are matched with a raw substring check on an address string.
why: This can attach a rule for 1 Chester Street to 11 Chester Street, and punctuation differences can also prevent a genuine match. PropertyDataService calls this matcher to populate the live Local Provisions card, so a property can be shown a site-only LEP rule that does not apply, or miss one that does.
fix: Normalise punctuation and compare parsed street-number and street/locality tokens exactly (prefer the available Lot/DP when present). Add tests for 1 versus 11 and comma/no-comma Portal address formats.

what: The provision-search query has no is_current or v2_is_actionable filter.
why: The repository defines the served rule set as current and actionable provisions. regulatory_provisions_canonical only denotes deduplication, so the active assessment search can return superseded or non-actionable text as a rule.
fix: Add the served-set predicates to both normal and ranked search paths, and test that retired/non-actionable fixtures are excluded.

what: When the legacy Python provision search exits unsuccessfully or cannot start, the API returns HTTP 200 with an empty successful result.
why: PostgreSQL search is feature-flagged and defaults off when USE_POSTGRESQL_PROVISIONS is unset. A missing interpreter, deployment-path error, or Python failure is therefore presented to users as “no provisions found,” silently hiding applicable rules.
fix: Reject on subprocess failure so the route returns a visible 5xx error, preserving the stderr only in server logs. Add tests for non-zero exit and spawn error.

what: The route validates and destructures lga, but drops it when building ProvisionSearchFilters; the database client has no LGA filter.
why: A caller that supplies an LGA can receive matching DCP/LEP provisions from other councils. That is especially unsafe in a planning product because identically named clauses and zones differ by council.
fix: Pass a normalised council key into the search client and filter by source_council; until that is implemented, reject lga requests rather than silently ignoring their jurisdiction. Cover both cases with route tests.

what: The primary property endpoint has no rate limit despite each request fanning out to Planning Portal, ArcGIS, and database lookups.
why: This is the address-entry endpoint used by the main assessment flow. Unbounded requests can exhaust server capacity or trigger upstream throttling, making legitimate property lookups fail.
fix: Apply the existing searchRateLimiter before starting the lookup, using the same client identifier and response headers as /api/property/profile. Add a 429 route test.

what: The legacy property route's Portal fetches have no timeout or abort signal.
why: Satellite and report routes depend on this endpoint. A Portal connection that accepts but never completes can hold their server request until platform timeout, rather than returning a controlled unavailable response.
fix: Use the existing fetchWithTimeout helper for address, lot, and layer requests, then add a stalled-fetch test asserting a bounded error response.

what: Unexpected property-lookup errors are returned to clients verbatim in details.
why: Database, upstream, and implementation error messages can disclose internal service structure while users only need to know that the lookup failed.
fix: Return a stable public error message and retain the detailed exception only in server logging/error tracking. Add a test using a simulated database error.
